pathways.name: CSF-facing implant surface colonization
pathways.description: Bacteria colonize the subarachnoid-facing surface of the eShunt tip, form biofilm, and cause ventriculitis/meningitis.
evidence_basis: The eShunt has a CSF-facing surface in the subarachnoid space — this surface is physically exposed to CSF, which has limited immune clearance.
0/66 infections at 90 days — but the CSF-facing surface biofilm pathway may take MONTHS to YEARS to manifest (VP shunt late infections occur at 6-24 months).
No published data on biofilm formation specifically on the eShunt's CSF-facing surface material.
The CSF-facing surface area is SMALLER than a VP shunt catheter (tip vs full catheter length), but the exact area is not published.
pathways.clinically_important: UNKNOWN — plausible but unobserved. The smaller surface area and the one-way valve (which prevents retrograde flow) may limit the clinical impact. But ventriculitis from even a small biofilm is a serious complication.
pathways.evidence_gap: Need: (1) long-term eShunt infection data, (2) eShunt tip material biofilm susceptibility testing, (3) CSF-facing surface area measurement

pathways.name: Venous implant surface colonization
pathways.description: Bacteria colonize the venous-facing surface of the eShunt (the valve and anchor in the sigmoid sinus), form biofilm, and cause endovascular infection or sepsis.
evidence_basis: The eShunt has a venous-facing surface in the sigmoid sinus — exposed to flowing venous blood.
Flowing blood has immune clearance (neutrophils, complement, immunoglobulins) — may reduce biofilm formation.
0/66 infections at 90 days — no endovascular infections observed.
Endovascular device infections (e.g., stent infections, pacemaker lead infections) are RARE (<1%) but DO occur, typically via hematogenous seeding.
The eShunt's venous surface is in a LOW-FLOW venous sinus (not a high-flow artery), which may reduce the wash-off effect.
pathways.clinically_important: LOW PROBABILITY — endovascular device infections are rare. The venous sinus is low-flow (may not provide as much wash-off as an artery), but the immune clearance in blood is still much higher than in CSF. If this pathway were clinically important, we would expect to see it in the 90-day data (endovascular infections typically manifest within weeks).
pathways.evidence_gap: Need: (1) long-term eShunt data for endovascular infection, (2) flow characterization in the sigmoid sinus, (3) comparison with other endovascular device infection rates

pathways.name: Hematogenous seeding
pathways.description: Bacteremia from any source (dental procedure, UTI, pneumonia, etc.) seeds the eShunt device, causing device infection.
evidence_basis: Hematogenous seeding is a known but RARE cause of VP shunt infection (~5% of late infections).
The eShunt's venous position means it is CONSTANTLY exposed to bloodstream bacteria — more so than a VP shunt catheter (which is in the relatively sterile CSF/peritoneum).
However, constant blood flow also means constant immune clearance — bacteria must survive the bloodstream AND adhere to the device AND form biofilm.
0/66 at 90 days — but hematogenous seeding is a LATE phenomenon (associated with transient bacteremia from dental work, infections, etc.).
Endovascular devices (stents, valves, pacemakers) do experience hematogenous seeding — rates are 0.1-1% per year for most devices.
pathways.clinically_important: LOW — hematogenous seeding rates for endovascular devices are 0.1-1% per year. This is an order of magnitude LOWER than VP shunt infection rates (5-10%). Even if the eShunt has the same hematogenous seeding rate as other endovascular devices, the residual burden would be SMALL.
pathways.evidence_gap: Need: (1) long-term eShunt data, (2) comparison with endovascular device hematogenous infection rates

pathways.name: Procedural contamination (implantation)
pathways.description: Bacteria introduced during the endovascular implantation procedure seed the device.
evidence_basis: 0/66 infections at 90 days — this DIRECTLY measures procedural contamination (early infections = procedural).
Standard endovascular sterile technique has <1% infection rate for vascular access procedures.
The eShunt procedure is performed in a cardiac catheterization lab / neurointerventional suite with standard sterile precautions.
The procedure is SHORTER than VP shunt surgery (endovascular access vs open cranial + abdominal surgery), reducing exposure time.
pathways.clinically_important: NO — 0/66 at 90 days directly demonstrates that procedural contamination is NOT a significant pathway for the eShunt. The early infection rate is OBSERVED to be zero.
pathways.evidence_gap: None — the 90-day data directly addresses this pathway. Procedural contamination is NOT a residual problem.

pathways.name: Delayed biofilm maturation
pathways.description: Low-grade bacterial contamination at implantation forms a slow-growing biofilm that takes months to years to cause clinical infection.
evidence_basis: Delayed biofilm maturation is a known phenomenon in VP shunts — late infections at 6-24 months are well-documented.
0/66 at 90 days does NOT capture this pathway (90 days is too short for delayed biofilm).

The eShunt's venous blood flow MAY prevent delayed biofilm maturation on the venous surface (constant immune clearance). But the CSF-facing surface is NOT exposed to blood flow and could still develop slow-growing biofilm.
No published data on long-term eShunt biofilm formation.
pathways.clinically_important: UNKNOWN — this is the SAME as P1 (CSF-facing biofilm) but with a longer timeline. If the CSF-facing surface can support slow-growing biofilm, delayed infection is possible. But the 90-day data shows NO early biofilm, which suggests either: (a) the device material is resistant, OR (b) biofilm has not had time to mature.
pathways.evidence_gap: Need: (1) long-term (>1 year) eShunt data, (2) in vitro biofilm testing of eShunt materials in CSF

pathway_P1_csf_biofilm.verdict: UNCERTAIN — cannot kill (plausible) and cannot promote (unobserved)

pathway_P2_venous_biofilm.verdict: NOT CONVINCING — the residual burden is likely too small to justify invention

pathway_P3_hematogenous.important: LOW — 0.1-1% per year for endovascular devices
pathway_P3_hematogenous.verdict: NOT CONVINCING — an order of magnitude lower than VP shunt infection

pathway_P4_procedural.verdict: KILLED — the 90-day data directly addresses this pathway

pathway_P5_delayed_biofilm.important: UNKNOWN — same as P1 but with longer timeline

decision.question: Is any eShunt-specific infection pathway both PHYSICALLY PLAUSIBLE and CLINICALLY IMPORTANT enough to justify invention work NOW?
decision.answer:
NO — not at this time.

The only UNCERTAIN pathways (P1 CSF-facing biofilm, P5 delayed biofilm) are physically plausible but have UNKNOWN clinical importance. They have NOT been observed in 66 patients at 90 days. The LOW-probability pathways (P2 venous biofilm, P3 hematogenous) are an order of magnitude less common than VP shunt infection. The procedural pathway (P4) is directly observed to be zero.

The machine CANNOT determine whether the CSF-facing biofilm pathway is clinically important without long-term data. But it also CANNOT justify invention work based on an unobserved, uncertain pathway.

The correct epistemic state is: the eShunt architecture eliminates the PRIMARY conventional infection pathway (transcutaneous track). The RESIDUAL pathways are either LOW probability (venous, hematogenous) or UNKNOWN (CSF-facing biofilm). No pathway is CONVINCING enough to justify mechanism generation NOW.

INF-001 is NOT KILLED (the residual is physically plausible) but is NOT PROMOTED (the residual is not clinically established). The problem is PARKED — it will be revisited if long-term eShunt data shows infection events.
decision.inf_001_verdict: PARKED — not killed, not promoted. The residual is physically plausible but not clinically established.
decision.action: Move to IIH-001 (Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension) — a different problem with higher technological leverage and a physically different mechanism.
what_would_revive_inf_001: Long-term (>1 year) eShunt data showing infection events
A specific patient population showing elevated eShunt infection risk
In vitro evidence that eShunt materials are highly susceptible to CSF biofilm
what_would_kill_inf_001_permanently: Long-term eShunt data showing continued 0 infections
Evidence that the CSF-facing surface is too small for clinically significant biofilm
Evidence that venous blood flow prevents biofilm maturation on the device

preserved_observations.vp_shunt_infection_rate: 4.75% adult pooled (2023 meta-analysis, prediction interval 1.19-17.1%); pediatric 5-15% — POPULATION-DEPENDENT
preserved_observations.eshunt_architecture_advantage: REMOVES ONE CONVENTIONAL PATHWAY (transcutaneous track) — not 'eliminates all infection risk'
